'''Friedhelm Waldhausen''' (born 1938 in [[:de:Millich|Millich]], [[Hückelhoven]], [[Rhine Province]], died November 21, 2024<ref>{{cite web|access-date=2025-06-30 |author=Moritz Kaßmann |language=de |publisher=Universität Bielefeld |title=Prof. Friedhelm Waldhausen verstorben |url=https://www.uni-bielefeld.de/fakultaeten/mathematik/dokumente/Waldhausen.pdf |website=Fakultät für Mathematik}}<!-- auto-translated from German by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>) was a German [[mathematician]] known for his work in [[algebraic topology]]. He made fundamental contributions in the fields of [[3-manifolds]] and (algebraic) [[K-theory]].

==Career==

Waldhausen studied mathematics at the [[University of Göttingen]], [[LMU Munich]], and the [[University of Bonn]]. He obtained his [[Ph.D.]] in 1966 from the [[University of Bonn]]; his advisor was [[Friedrich Hirzebruch]] and his thesis was entitled "Eine Klasse von 3-dimensionalen Mannigfaltigkeiten" (A class of 3-dimensional manifolds).<ref>{{MathGenealogy|24057}}</ref>

After visits to [[Princeton University]], the [[University of Illinois]], and the [[University of Michigan]] he moved in 1968 to [[Kiel University]], where he completed his habilitation (qualified to assume a professorship).

In 1969, he was appointed professor at the [[Ruhr University Bochum]] before in 1971 becoming a professor at [[Bielefeld University]], an appointment he held until his retirement in 2004.<ref>{{cite book|author = Winfried Scharlau|title=Das Glück, Mathematiker zu sein: Friedrich Hirzebruch und seine Zeit (Deutsch)|page = 134| url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007%2F978-3-658-14757-0_16.pdf|doi=10.1007/978-3-658-14757-0_16}}</ref><ref name="Kontakt (Universität Bielefeld)">{{cite web | title=PEVZ: Fakultät für Mathematik / Emeriti / Professorinnen und Professoren im Ruhestand | website=Kontakt (Universität Bielefeld) | url=https://ekvv.uni-bielefeld.de/pers_publ/publ/EinrichtungDetail.jsp?orgId=13021752 | language=de | access-date=17 December 2021}}</ref>

==Academic work==

His early work was mainly on the theory of [[3-manifold]]s. He dealt mainly with [[Haken manifold]]s and [[Heegaard splitting]]. Among other things, he proved that, roughly speaking, any homotopy equivalence of Haken manifolds is homotopic to a homeomorphism, i.e. that closed Haken manifolds are topologically rigid. He put forward the [[Waldhausen conjecture]] about Heegaard splitting.

In the mid-seventies, he extended the connection between geometric topology and [[algebraic K-theory]] by introducing A-theory, a kind of algebraic K-theory for topological spaces. This led to new foundations for algebraic K-theory (using what are now called [[Waldhausen category|Waldhausen categories]]) and also gave new impetus to the study of highly structured [[Ring spectrum (homotopy theory)|ring spectra]].

==Recognition==

Today, Waldhausen is seen, together with [[Daniel Quillen]], as one of the pioneers of algebraic [[K-theory]]. Among others, he was awarded the von [[Staudt Prize]] in 2004 along with [[Günter Harder]], and an honorary doctorate from [[Osnabrück University]].<ref>[https://www.uni-osnabrueck.de/fileadmin/documents/public/1_universitaet/1.2_zahlen_daten_fakten/vpv/pv_SoSe_2019_Mai.pdf Honorary doctorate Osnabrück]</ref>

==Important publications==
*''Algebraic <math>K</math>-theory of spaces, Algebraic and geometric topology ''(New Brunswick, N.J., 1983), 318–419, Lecture Notes in Math., 1126, Springer, Berlin, 1985.
*''Algebraic <math>K</math>-theory of spaces, concordance, and stable homotopy theory, Algebraic topology and algebraic <math>K</math>-theory'' (Princeton, N.J., 1983), 392–417, Ann.  of Math. Stud., 113, Princeton Univ. Press, Princeton, NJ, 1987.
*(with Marcel Bökstedt) ''The map <math>BSG\to A(*)\to QS^0</math>, Algebraic topology and algebraic <math>K</math>-theory'' (Princeton, N.J., 1983), 418–431, Ann. of Math. Stud., 113, Princeton Univ. Press, Princeton, NJ, 1987.
